opening.headline: When you want to make responses faster and cheaper, learn how to break down where the delay is coming from and choose the most effective measures first.
body: Let's say your service is slow to respond and your monthly bill is growing, so you want to reduce both. There are many candidate vehicles. Smaller models, shorter outputs, caching, parallel calls, and batching are all possible. However, each method has a different effect, and if you spend time on something that has little effect, you will not feel it.

In this lesson, we break down latency into its components to see which section is larger, and organize where model grade, output length, caching, and parallelism are effective. Next, we compare cases where the same method works and cases where it does not work, and practice distinguishing between the most effective methods.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain optimization techniques to reduce latency and costs
You can distinguish which means are most effective among model class, output length, caching, and parallelization.

screens.title: Want to make responses faster and cheaper
screens.lead: Read one team's concerns and think about where to start.

visual.alt: A scene where five candidate means are placed with question marks.

paragraphs: The response of a service created by one team is slow for users, and monthly bills are getting bigger. The team would like to reduce both. There are five candidates that emerged from the meeting: switching to a smaller model, shortening the output, turning on caching, sending multiple calls in parallel, and sending non-delay-requiring tasks in batches.

The problem is that each method has different effects. If you spend a week refining your input prompts and it doesn't make much of a difference in how fast you feel, that effort was wasted without much benefit.

So optimization begins with measurement, not selection of means. If you know where your time is being spent, you can start cutting back on the biggest sections. The question in this class is where to start to get the most benefit.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: If I cut the input prompts in half, would the response time also be cut in half? I'll answer again at the end of class.

screens.outro: First, let me recall where things were slow in my experience.

screens.title: Think back: Where was it slow?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: What was your first suspicion when you noticed a slow response?
items.answer: Many people's first suspicion is the length of the input prompt. However, in most cases, most of the time is spent on the steps that produce the output. You need to get into the habit of measuring before doubting.

items.prompt: Have you ever experienced reducing the prompts but not feeling much of it?
items.answer: Reducing input makes sense on cost, but has little impact on latency unless you have a very large context. The experience is not unusual, but a normal result of the configuration of the delay.

items.prompt: Aren't you using the largest model for all requests?
items.answer: The largest models are comfortable, but are usually slower and more expensive. By splitting enough requests into small models, considering the quality required for each request, both delay and cost can be reduced.

screens.outro: Now that we've gathered our experience, let's break down what lag consists of.

screens.title: Components of Latency
screens.lead: Move the sliders to see the components that make up the delay one by one. It's good to note how big each element is in the overall delay.

visual.alt: Horizontal bar plot of latency stacked by component.
labels: Reducing the output by half also roughly halves the delay.
Even if the input is reduced by half, it is around 1~5%.

stops.body: Latency is the time it takes the model to process a prompt and produce output. Model size, prompt complexity, and infrastructure have an impact. This time is not a single chunk, but is divided into several sections, and the method of reducing it is different for each section.

TTFT is the time until the first token is issued. It determines the responsiveness that users experience while streaming. Longer input processing increases this time, so input reduction and caching can benefit TTFT in very long contexts.

Generating output tokens is almost always the longest step. Because tokens are generated one by one in sequence, halving the output tokens roughly halves the delay. The first candidate for reducing delay is the length of the output.
Halving the input tokens can only improve latency by 1 to 5 percent. The effect is small unless you have a very large context. Reducing input has greater cost implications than delay.

Since each request causes a round-trip delay, the number of requests also adds to the delay. If you're sending calls sequentially that don't depend on each other, you can significantly reduce the overall time by making them parallel.

screens.outro: Now that we've disassembled the components, let's summarize the principles for reducing them.

screens.title: Latency Reduction Techniques: Seven Principles
screens.lead: As you select each item, an explanation of the principles for reducing latency will unfold. Open them all and think about which principles will be most important to your service.

items.title: Process it faster
items.body: Smaller models are usually faster and cheaper. Choosing the smallest model that matches the quality required by your request will reduce both delays and costs.

items.title: Generate Few Tokens
items.body: Generating output takes the longest, so let it speak only as much as necessary. The prompt asks for a concise answer and places an upper bound on max_tokens. Structured output reduces the syntax itself by shortening function names and argument names.

items.title: Write fewer input tokens
items.body: Fewer inputs reduce costs and, in very large contexts, also reduce delays. The effect on delay is less than reducing output, so give it a low priority.

items.title: Reduce the number of requests
items.body: Each request adds round-trip delay. Seeing if you can do multiple tasks at once will reduce overall time.

items.title: Parallelization
items.body: Break non-sequential steps into parallel calls. Steps that inevitably follow sequentially can be accelerated in part by speculative execution. It works great if you have multiple calls that don't depend on each other.

items.title: Make users wait less
items.body: Streaming, step marking, and loading states do not reduce actual time, but they do reduce perceived waiting. If the first token is seen quickly, the user knows a response is on the way and is less anxious.

items.title: Don't use LLM as default
items.body: Problems solved by rules are handled by code. The code is much faster and cheaper than model calls. Gathering the prefixes in front benefits the KV cache and also reduces input processing.

screens.outro: Now that we've covered the principles, let's look at model classes and output lengths in detail.

screens.title: Select model class and limit output length
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn how to adjust model rating and output length.

tabs.label: Choose a lightweight model
tabs.body: If speed is important, use a lightweight model like Claude Haiku 5.5 and adjust speed and cost with effort. If you use a model that is too large for the quality required by the request, delays and costs will be greater than necessary. For tasks like classification, extraction, and short summarization, lightweight models are often sufficient.

tabs.label: Quality Complementary
tabs.body: The quality of small models can be complemented by more detailed prompts, few-shot examples, and fine-tuning. So, when changing to a small model, rather than immediately returning to the large model because of lack of quality, it is better to supplement it with prompts and examples first.

tabs.label: Output length limit
tabs.body: Ask for a concise answer directly at the prompt, and cap the output with max_tokens. Since the answer may be truncated if only an upper limit is given, it is written with instructions to be concise. In structured output, the syntax itself is shortened by shortening function names and argument names.

tabs.label: Common strategies of OpenAI
tabs.body: OpenAI documentation cites reducing the number of requests, minimizing tokens, and selecting smaller models as common strategies to reduce cost and delay. All three work in the same direction. Reducing tokens and requests reduces both cost and delay. These three are a common starting point even if the services are different.

screens.outro: Let us now compare cost-side optimization with organizational-level principles.

screens.title: Cost optimization and AI/ML cost principles
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare the costs of reducing them at the request level versus managing them at the organization level.

states.label: Request-level cost savings
states.body: The Gemini article compares the costs of different processing methods. Flex and Batch are 50% off, and caching is 90% off, but storage costs are separate. Priority is 75 to 100 percent higher than standard. In other words, the unit price varies greatly depending on how the same request is processed. Cost and delay largely go together, so reducing tokens and requests reduces both. OpenAI's production best practices also address usage limits and cost management.

states.label: Organization-level cost principles
states.body: Google Cloud has five AI·ML cost principles: Define and measure costs and revenue, optimize resource allocation, have data management and governance, automate MLOps, and leverage managed services and pre-trained models. Costs are tracked in detail with billing reports, budgets, notifications, and monitoring. Request-level techniques are a means within this principle. You need to look at both levels to know whether a reduction in one request translates into lower costs for the organization as a whole. We also check whether savings techniques do not compromise service quality or safety.

screens.outro: Now that we've covered all the concepts, let's start with examples that work well.

screens.title: Explanatory Case: When Lightweight Models and Caching Work
screens.lead: The instructor explains the case step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: A long system prompt is followed by a short classification question, and the output is a single line of labels. We are currently using a large model and processing hundreds of thousands of requests per day. Costs are high and response is slow.

steps.title: Step 1: Break down the sources of costs
steps.body: Most of the big costs of large models come from repeated long prefixes and unnecessarily large models. The output is one line, so the output cost and generation time are already small. So the places to reduce are the input and model ratings.

steps.title: Step 2: Fix the prefix and change the model
steps.body: Use the cache by fixing the prefix in front and change it to a lightweight model. Cache hits are high because system prompts are repeated, and classification is something a lightweight model can do well.

steps.title: Step 3: Check the effect
steps.body: Because the output is a short label, the creation time is short, and both model replacement and caching are highly effective. Caching reduces input costs, and lightweight models reduce unit costs and processing times, reducing both costs and delays.

steps.title: Step 4: Complement and verify quality
steps.body: Complement the quality of the lightweight model with a few-shot example and check the results. Compare representative examples to see if the classification accuracy is similar to that of a model with high classification accuracy. If accuracy is lacking, increase examples or reinforce prompts, and only send some of the requests that are still lacking to the larger model. Dividing requests by level of difficulty in this way ensures both quality and cost.

steps.title: organizing
steps.body: In this case, caching and lightweight models worked because the sources of cost were input iterations and large models. This is the result of disassembling where the bottleneck is and then selecting appropriate measures. Remember that even for the same service, if there are requests with long output, those requests require different means.

data.notes: There is only one conclusion. Break down where most of the delay comes from and reduce it starting from the largest section. It's normal for the same tool to work great for some requests and barely work for others. The effectiveness of the means depends on the nature of the request. If a service contains a mix of requests of various types, it is recommended to create a table for each type of request and determine the means separately. You should also check whether response quality is maintained after changing means. Even if it is faster and cheaper, if the quality is poor, the optimization is not successful.

screens.outro: I will gather the analysis and summarize the key points.

screens.title: Key takeaway: Select a sentence and check the evidence
screens.lead: If you select each summary sentence, the evidence will unfold. There is nothing to enter or submit.

items.prompt: A big part of the delay is output token generation, so reducing the output length has a big effect.
items.answer: Halving the output tokens roughly halves the delay. It asks for concise answers, places an upper bound on max_tokens, and structured output shortens the syntax by shortening names.

items.prompt: Reducing input has greater cost implications than delay, and caching and prefix fixation help.
items.answer: Reducing the input by half may only improve latency by a few percent. However, the cost is reduced, and by gathering the prefix upfront, the KV cache reduces input processing.

items.prompt: Model rank, output length, caching, and parallelization have different effects depending on the situation.
items.answer: If you have long repeated prefixes, you have caching, if you have short outputs, you have a lightweight model, and if you have multiple calls that don't depend on each other, there's a lot of parallelism. The effectiveness of either means will depend on the nature of the request.

items.prompt: Break down where the delay is coming from and then reduce it starting from the largest section.
items.answer: Measurement comes first. You need to know which section is larger: input processing, output generation, or number of requests. If you choose the means first, it is easy to waste time on things that have little effect.

screens.outro: Lastly, let's think about it in relation to our own work.

screens.title: Connect to my work
screens.lead: This screen is for reading only. Read the questions and think for yourself. You will not enter or submit an answer.

paragraphs: Key terms in this lesson are reducing latency, selecting model classes, limiting output length, and optimizing cost. Let's go back to the original question. If I halved the input prompts, would the response time also be halved? Not unless it's a very large context. The improvement may be only 1 to 5 percent.

Thinking about your service, estimate the time of a request by dividing it into the round trip of the request, processing the input, and generating the output. Knowing where the biggest sections are will help you decide where to tackle them first. Most often it is output generation.

Then choose the method that suits that section. It is an output limiting model if the output is long, parallelization if there are many calls, caching if the prefix is ​​repeated, and a lightweight model if the required quality is low. Instead of changing everything at once, change them one by one and measure the effects.
Track your expenses separately. You'll need to see changes in your billing reports, budgets, and alerts to know if your optimizations have actually reduced costs.

callout.label: Questions to Think About
callout.text: Where does my business stand when it comes to reducing latency? Think about where the slowest requests spend their time.

checks.q: Services that generate long reports are slow to respond. Which method is most likely to reduce delays?
options: Reduce the output length. Halving the output tokens can roughly halve the delay.
Halve the input tokens. Delay is reduced by approximately half.
Inputs and outputs do not affect latency, so only the server location is checked.
Share the same work by doubling the number of requests
checks.explain: Generating output tokens is almost always the longest step. Even if you reduce the input by half, the delay improvement can only be about 1-5%.

wrong.1: Even if you reduce the input tokens, the delay improvement is small unless you have a very large context.
wrong.2: Both input and output tokens affect delay, with output having a particularly large impact.
wrong.3: Since each request adds round-trip delay, increasing the number of requests can be disadvantageous.

checks.intro: This is a report generation service that is slow to respond. Determine where the biggest cause of delay is.
checks.correctFeedback: That's right. Since output token generation is the longest step, reducing the output length has the greatest effect on delay.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Inputs and outputs have different effects on delay. Remember that even if you halve the input, the improvement may only be 1-5%.

checks.q: A long system prompt is followed by a short classification question, and the output is a one-line label. What is the most appropriate combination of reducing both cost and delay?
options: Significantly increase the output upper limit, allowing the model to make more detailed judgments
Put the request time at the beginning of the system prompt and turn on caching.
Keep the large model and further reduce max_tokens
Fix the prefix in front for caching and change to a lightweight model, but complement the quality with few-shot examples.
checks.explain: The cost comes from repeated long prefixes and unnecessarily large models. Prefix fixation, caching, and a lightweight model are correct, and few-shot examples complement the quality.

wrong.0: Since the output is already one line, there is no reason to increase it, and it only increases costs and delays.
wrong.1: If there is a changing value in the beginning, the prefix does not match and the cache is not reused.
wrong.2: Since the output is already short, adjusting max_tokens has little effect.

checks.intro: Look for costs and delays in the features of long prefixes and single-line output.
checks.correctFeedback: That's right. It is a combination of caching repeated prefixes, replacing excessive models with lightweight models, and supplementing quality with few-shot examples.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Increasing the output upper limit or putting the changing value first will actually reduce the effect. Start from the point that repeated long prefixes and large models are the source of cost.

checks.q: Match the measures you would look at first in the following situations:
left: The prefix varies for each question.
This is a task that requires complex reasoning.
There are multiple calls that do not depend on each other
right: Before switching to a lightweight model, consider reinforcing effort and prompts.
Since the caching effect is small, look at parallelism and model rating first.
Look at output length restrictions or restructuring first.
checks.explain: Each method has a different effect. Break down where the delay is coming from and reduce it starting from the largest section.
checks.intro: Depending on the cause of the delay, the means to look first will vary. Match the situation with the means.
checks.correctFeedback: That's correct. You demonstrated the mindset of breaking down where delays come from and choosing the most effective means first.
checks.incorrectFeedback: There is a mismatched pair. If the output is long, adjust the length, if the prefix changes every time, parallelize or model grade instead of caching, and if it is complex inference, check effort first before lowering the model.

glossary.def: A set of techniques to reduce model processing speed, number of output tokens, number of requests, parallelization, and user perceived latency.
The decision is to choose the smallest model that meets the required quality, thereby reducing both delay and cost.
A concise response request and upper limit on max_tokens is a way to reduce the longest output generation step.
It involves adjusting tokens, requests, processing ranks, and caching to achieve the same result at lower cost.
Principles outlined by Google Cloud include cost and revenue measurement, resource allocation, data governance, MLOps, and leveraging managed services.

misconceptions.myth: Reducing the input prompts will significantly reduce lag.
misconceptions.fact: Reducing the input by half may only improve latency by a few percent. Most of the delay comes from output generation.

misconceptions.myth: The largest model is always the safe choice.
misconceptions.fact: A smaller model for the job is faster and cheaper. Quality can be complemented by prompts, few-shot examples, and fine-tuning.
It is only effective when the prefix is repeated and matches. If the prefix is ​​different for each question, the effect is small.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.

Break down where the delay is coming from and then reduce it starting from the largest section.
